title: Old treasure and new (Matthew 13:44–58)
hook: a shovel hits something in a field, and a storeroom holds new and old
tomorrow: how do you show up for people on your own sad day?

segments.voice: Last time, a field of wheat and weeds, and an owner who wouldn't let anyone rip them out early. Let both grow. Now, something hidden in a field.

Saturday at an estate sale: a shoebox of someone's old records on a card table, and next to it, a brand-new speaker still in plastic. Come for one, leave with both. Now a field, a long time ago. A man is digging, and his shovel hits something hard. He brushes the dirt away, looks, and covers it right back up. Then he walks home and starts selling everything he owns. Every last thing. Matthew gives his reason in three words.
screen: `OLD RECORDS, A NEW SPEAKER.` → `A SHOVEL HITS SOMETHING.` → `HE SELLS EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: The words are: "for joy thereof." Nobody's forcing him. He isn't giving things up; he's found something worth more than all of it, and he buys the field. A merchant does the same for one pearl. Then, after a net full of every kind of fish, Jesus checks in: "Have ye understood all these things? They say unto him, Yea, Lord." And he gives them one last picture, about themselves: "every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old." A scribe is someone trained in the scriptures. The householder doesn't empty the storeroom to restock it. He reaches in for both. Here's the cliffhanger. The very next scene puts Jesus in his own hometown, in the synagogue, and the people there can't get past the old: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" They name his mother and his brothers. They know his face so well they can't see anything new in it. He answers: "A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house." And Matthew ends the chapter quietly: "he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief." One storeroom held new and old. One hometown only had room for the old.
screen: `FOR JOY THEREOF.` · `HAVE YE UNDERSTOOD?` · `THINGS NEW AND OLD.` · `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER'S SON?`

segments.voice: Say out loud, quietly, one old thing you'd never give up: a song, a recipe, a saying from someone who raised you. Then say one new thing you've found this year and are glad of. Breathe with the two of them side by side, out of the same storeroom.
Old treasure and new. The householder's storeroom in Matthew 13, where neither gets thrown out to make room for the other.
Worth keeping: new and old, from one treasure, in one pair of hands. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches sing old hymns and new songs in the same service, and some Christians point to Matthew 13:52 when they speak of keeping what's handed down while welcoming what's new.

'A scribe is someone trained in the scriptures' is a plain gloss; confirm it is fair.
'One pearl of great price' in the match game follows KJV 13:46. The net parable (13:47–50) is named only in passing.
